title: The Road Racing Guide
subtitle: Everything you need to train for and race gran fondos, sportives, and centuries.
meta_description: A complete road racing training guide — from building your aerobic engine to pack tactics, fueling, and race-week execution. Written by coaches who race.

glossary.FTP: Functional Threshold Power — the highest power you can sustain for roughly an hour. The anchor for training zones and the number every other number is a percentage of.
glossary.W/kg: Watts per kilogram — power divided by body weight. The currency of climbing: on a steep col, W/kg is speed.
glossary.CTL: Chronic Training Load — a rolling average of your daily training stress over roughly six weeks. A proxy for fitness.
glossary.ATL: Acute Training Load — the same average over roughly seven days. A proxy for fatigue.
glossary.TSB: Training Stress Balance — CTL minus ATL. Positive means fresh, negative means loaded. Race day wants it positive.
glossary.TSS: Training Stress Score — a single number combining how long and how hard a ride was. 100 TSS is roughly one hour all-out at threshold.
glossary.IF: Intensity Factor — a ride's normalized power divided by your FTP. How hard the ride was, relative to you.
glossary.NP: Normalized Power — a power average weighted to account for surges and variability. Closer to a ride's true physiological cost than plain average power.
glossary.RPE: Rating of Perceived Exertion — how hard an effort feels, usually on a 1-10 scale. The cheapest power meter you own.
glossary.Z2: Zone 2 — the conversational endurance intensity (roughly 56-75% of FTP) where most of your training hours belong.
glossary.VO2max: Your body's maximum rate of oxygen uptake. Trained with short, very hard intervals; it sets the ceiling your threshold lives under.
glossary.PMC: Performance Management Chart — the graph that plots CTL, ATL, and TSB over time so you can see fitness, fatigue, and freshness in one place.
glossary.DOMS: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness — the ache that arrives 24-48 hours after unaccustomed effort.
glossary.bonk: The abrupt collapse that happens when your body runs out of stored carbohydrate. Preventable. See Chapter 5.
glossary.echelon: The diagonal paceline that forms in a crosswind, where shelter sits beside and behind the rider ahead instead of directly behind. When the road runs out of width, the race splits.
glossary.autobus: The survival group that forms at the back on hard days — in pro races, the sprinters' bus riding together to beat the time cut. Organized, unhurried, and usually good company.
glossary.feed zone: A designated stretch of course where events hand up bottles and food. Plan for chaos: slow down, grab, and don't stop at the first table.
glossary.broom wagon: The vehicle at the back of an event that collects riders outside the time cut. Its arrival is polite but non-negotiable.
glossary.neutral start: The controlled opening kilometres behind a lead vehicle before racing officially begins. Not the place to move up — and rarely as easy as advertised.
glossary.gran fondo: Italian for 'big ride' — a mass-start, chip-timed road event, typically 100-200 km with real climbing. Raced from the front, ridden everywhere else.
glossary.sportive: The British and northern-European cousin of the gran fondo — often completion-focused, sometimes segment-timed rather than raced gun-to-line.
glossary.cat: Racing category. Licensed road racing groups riders into cats — you move up by finishing races and scoring points.
glossary.UCI Gran Fondo World Series: The worldwide qualification circuit of gran fondos: finish high enough in your age group at a qualifier and you earn a start at the UCI Gran Fondo World Championships.

chapters.title: What Is Road Racing?
chapters.subtitle: Fondos, sportives, and the events you're actually training for

blocks.content: Road racing, for most of us, means the mass-participation events that have exploded over the last two decades: gran fondos, sportives, centuries, the big timed climbs. You're not racing a 90-rider pro peloton. You're chasing a number on a finish-line clock, a personal best, or the wheel of the rider who dropped you last year.

What makes the road different from gravel or the trail is the pack. Drafting is the whole game — sit in the right wheel and you save 25-30% of your energy; get caught in the wind alone and the day falls apart. The surface is predictable; the tactics are not. Positioning, timing, and knowing when to spend your matches matter more than raw watts.

The clock doesn't grade on effort. A gran fondo has chip timing, a results page, and a finish-line photo you didn't pose for. Whether you call your day a race is up to you — the event will treat it like one either way.

This guide is built around that reality: an aerobic engine big enough to finish strong, the threshold to hold a hard group, and the handling to stay safe and efficient in a bunch. Everything here is written by coaches who actually pin numbers on.

"Road racing" is an umbrella over events that share pavement and almost nothing else. A flat century and a Dolomites gran fondo are different sports that happen to use the same bike. Before you train for "road racing," know which one you actually signed up for — because the event type determines the plan, the fueling, and which chapters of this guide will save your day.

blocks.caption: The Event Landscape
rows: Mass-start, chip-timed, usually with serious climbing. Raced hard at the front, ridden everywhere else
The British and northern-European cousin — completion-focused, often segment-timed rather than raced gun-to-line

blocks.content: At one end of the spectrum sits the mountain gran fondo — the format that built the sport in Europe and the one most people mean when they say they're "training for a big one":
At the other end, the randonneuring tradition, where the question isn't how fast you can ride but whether you can keep riding at all:

Licensed racing — criteriums, road races, the cat system — is its own ladder with its own rulebook, and mostly beyond this guide's scope. But the skills overlap almost completely. Chapter 6 is the same chapter a first-year cat 5 needs; the fondo just gives you more time to make friends.

Everything downstream — the plan you follow, the food you carry, the skills you practice — inherits from the event you choose. That choice is the whole of Chapter 2. For now, one honest question: which of these events do you actually want, as opposed to the one your group chat picked?

Before you pick a race or a plan, be honest about the raw material: the hours you will actually train, not the hours you intend to. These four profiles run through the whole guide — later chapters serve different advice depending on which one you pick, so pick the one that matches your calendar, not your self-image.

tabs.label: Autobus
tabs.title: The Autobus (0-5 hrs/week)
tabs.content:
In a pro race, the autobus is the group that forms at the back on mountain days — sprinters, domestiques, and anyone having a bad one, organized around a single goal: finish inside the time cut. It is not a failure state. It is a working system with rules, experienced drivers, and a proud tradition of getting everyone home.

If you're training 0-5 hours a week for a big road event, this is your bus. The plan is damage control: enough riding to finish, ruthless pacing so that hour two doesn't write a check hour five can't cash, and zero heroics.

**Training reality:** 0-5 hours per week. Underprepared by conventional standards — and you know it. The plan's job is to get you to the line anyway.

tabs.label: Finisher
tabs.title: The Finisher (5-12 hrs/week)
tabs.content:
Finishers sign up for the big one — [Mallorca 312](/race/mallorca-312/), [L'Étape du Tour](/race/letape-du-tour/) — and want to finish strong, not crawl in. This is most first-time fondo riders, and it is the right ambition: strong enough to enjoy the last 30 km instead of merely surviving them.

**Training reality:** 5-12 hours per week. Enough for a real base and a real build without surrendering your job, your weekends, or your marriage. Most of this guide is written with you in mind.

tabs.label: Sharp End
tabs.title: The Sharp End (12-18 hrs/week)
tabs.content:
The sharp end is the front of the local chaingang and the first start pen at the fondo. You're not just finishing — you're racing the course, the clock, and a handful of specific people you would never admit you're racing.

**Training reality:** 12-18 hours per week. At this volume the limiter flips: recovery, not training, is the thing you have to get right. Structure stops being optional, and the gray zone (Chapter 4) becomes your most expensive habit.

tabs.label: Racer
tabs.title: The Racer (18+ hrs/week)
tabs.content:
Licensed, or effectively licensed: results are the point. Age-group podiums, UCI Gran Fondo qualification, the pointy end of whatever you enter. Little in this guide will be new to you in concept — the value is in execution, and in the race-craft chapters most training resources skip.

**Training reality:** 18+ hours per week across periodized blocks. Every session has a purpose, and the calendar is built around the season. Ideally your family has agreed to this.

blocks.content: Pick where you are, not where you'd like to be. A Sharp End plan on Autobus hours doesn't make you faster — it makes you tired, then injured, then absent. The archetypes exist so the advice fits the life you're actually training in.

Road events demand four things, in roughly this order:

**An aerobic engine.** Even the "short" events run for hours. The engine — built slowly, mostly at conversational pace — is what lets you produce power deep into a long day. There is no workaround and no product that replaces it.

**A threshold you can lean on.** The climbs, the crosswind sections, and the moments a group splits are all decided at or near your {{FTP}}. The bigger it is relative to your weight, the more of the race happens below your panic line.

**Pack skills.** Free speed, measured in whole percentages. Riding a wheel well, holding position without surging, and reading the group are learnable skills that most riders never deliberately practice.

**Durability.** Not just finishing — still functioning at hour five. The rider who fades least usually beats the rider who was fastest at hour one.

items.label: Fitness
items.detail: Costs nothing but time. The engine decides whether you're in the group or watching it ride away.

items.label: Pack craft & positioning
items.detail: The same watts can finish 20 minutes apart depending on where they're spent. Free speed for anyone willing to practice it.

items.label: Pacing
items.detail: You can be fit and still detonate on the first col. Discipline early buys speed late.

items.label: Fueling
items.detail: Bonking is a fueling failure, not a fitness one. Cheap to fix, catastrophic to ignore.

items.label: Equipment
items.detail: Real, but last. Aero gains are worth minutes; everything above is worth hours.

blocks.context: Energy saved sitting in a good draft at speed. The largest free speed in the sport — and it's a skill, not a purchase.

blocks.content: Notice what sits at the bottom of that list. Road cycling is the most equipment-obsessed corner of the sport, and the order above does not care. Deep wheels and an aero frame are real speed — a fraction of what the draft gives you for free, and a rounding error next to the engine. Buy fitness first. It's cheaper, and nobody has ever stolen it from a roof rack.

Equipment sits at the bottom of the hierarchy — but you still have to buy some, and road cycling's marketing department would like a word with your savings. Here is the honest priority order. The pattern to notice: everything near the top is about *fit, reliability, and contact with the bike*, and everything the ads push hardest lives near the bottom.

blocks.content: And the best equipment money you'll spend isn't a component at all: it's a professional bike fit. Road riding means hours in essentially one position — a fit that lets you stay in the drops comfortably is worth real watts (aero you can actually hold beats aero you bought), and it prevents the numb hands, hot feet, and grumpy lower backs that end more long days than fitness ever does. Get the fit before the wheels. Get the fit before most things.

items.title: Gearing for the mountains
items.content: If the course climbs seriously and you're debating cassettes, take the easier one. Nobody has ever crested a col wishing their gears were harder, and a 34t (or bigger) sprocket lets you keep a rideable cadence at the gradients where fondos are lost. Modern drivetrains accommodate wide ranges without drama — spin the climbs, save the knees, drop nobody's respect.

items.title: Tires, the short version
items.content: The modern consensus is friendly to comfort: wider tires (28-30mm on most rims) at moderate pressures roll as fast or faster than the old narrow-and-rock-hard setup, and they corner and descend better — which on an alpine course is time, not just comfort. Buy supple over light, match pressure to your weight and width rather than to tradition, and settle your exact setup in training. Race day inherits it; it doesn't audition it.

items.title: Do you need a power meter?
items.content: Need? No — Chapter 3's zones work off heart rate and RPE, and riders raced brilliantly for a century without wattage. But if you're training seriously, it's the best measurement money you can spend: precise interval targets, honest pacing on long climbs, and a record that makes Chapter 8's debrief factual instead of impressionistic. A basic single-sided unit does the whole job.

blocks.content: Every upgrade competes with the training it could have bought. The industry sells watts in boxes; most of yours are still in your legs, at a much better price per watt.

sections.title: The Honest Answer to "Can I Finish?"

blocks.content:
Almost certainly — with caveats that scale with the course. A flat-to-rolling century off 14-18 weeks of consistent training from a real base is a very achievable first goal; Chapter 2 covers the runway math. The pack helps you here: a steady group at conversational effort moves faster than you'd believe, and events are built to carry first-timers home.

Mountain fondos are a different contract. Time cuts are real and enforced by the {{broom wagon}}. Long alpine descents demand bike handling that flat-land training never teaches. Weather at 2,000 metres does not read the forecast you packed for. None of this is a reason not to go — it is a reason to respect the runway and pick the right first event.
Distance isn't the only axis, either. The spring-classics sportives trade altitude for violence — cobbles, bergs, and weather — and beat you up more per kilometre than anything with a col in it:

blocks.question: You want to finish a mountain gran fondo comfortably next season. Which factor best predicts how your day goes?

options.text: The weight and price of your bike
Your weight-adjusted threshold power and the discipline to pace the climbs
Your best 30-second sprint power

blocks.explanation: On a climbing course, gravity is the tax collector: W/kg sets your climbing speed, and pacing discipline decides whether you can hold it on the last col as well as the first. Equipment shifts the result by low single-digit percentages. The engine, and how you spend it, decides the rest.

blocks.content:
Mass-participation road racing is the most accessible version of bike racing there is: no license, no team, no tactics meeting — a course, a clock, and you. It is also deeper than it looks. The pack is chess at 40 km/h, the mountains don't negotiate, and the difference between a good day and a very long one is mostly decisions you can learn in advance.

That's what the rest of this guide is: the decisions, in order. Next up — [choosing the race](/guide/choosing-your-race/) that fits the engine you have and the life you're training in.

chapters.title: Choosing Your Race
chapters.subtitle: Pick the event that fits your engine and your calendar

blocks.content: The race you pick determines the plan you need. A flat 100-mile fondo rewards sustained tempo and pack craft; a mountainous sportive with 10,000 ft of climbing rewards a high power-to-weight and the discipline to ride your own pace up the cols. Pick the demands first, then build toward them.

Most riders do this backwards. They pick the event with the best photos, register in a January enthusiasm spike, and only later discover what the course actually asks of them. This chapter is the antidote: a way to read a race's demands before you commit, and to match them against the two resources you can't fake — your engine and your calendar.

Every road event is a bundle of demands, and you can read most of them off the route page: total distance, total climbing, how the climbing is distributed, altitude, and what the weather does there in that month. Two numbers do most of the work. The first is distance, which sets the duration of your day and therefore the fueling and durability problem. The second — more predictive than distance on any hilly course — is **metres of climbing per kilometre of route**. A course that climbs 30 metres per kilometre is a climbing race that happens to have flat bits. A course at 9 m/km is a rouleur's race where the climbs are punchy interruptions.

Two Tier 1 monuments make the point. The [Maratona dles Dolomites](/race/maratona-dles-dolomites/) packs 4,230 m of climbing into 138 km — over 30 m/km, a day spent almost entirely going up or coming down. The [Tour of Flanders Sportive](/race/tour-of-flanders-sportive/) climbs 2,260 m across 241 km — around 9 m/km, but delivered in short, brutal cobbled bergs where position into the base decides your whole effort. Same sport on paper. Different bodies, different plans, different chapters of this guide doing the heavy lifting.

blocks.content: Altitude deserves its own line. Events that spend real time above 2,000 metres tax you in ways sea-level training can't fully prepare — expect your power at altitude to be meaningfully down, and pace accordingly. If the profile shows long stretches at elevation and you live at sea level, that's not a dealbreaker. It's a pacing instruction.

Give yourself runway. A first century or fondo wants 14-18 weeks from a real base; if you're starting from the couch, more. Slot one A-event per season and build everything around it — B-events become hard training days, not goals that fragment your focus.

"A real base" means you are already riding several times a week, comfortably, and have been for a couple of months. It does not mean fast — it means consistent. If that's not you yet, the honest move is to add 8-12 weeks of easy, frequent riding before the 14-18 week plan even starts. The event date doesn't care when you registered; it only cares what you did between then and now.

steps.label: Base (weeks 1-6)
steps.content: Mostly easy volume, building the aerobic engine. The long ride grows steadily. Intensity is sparse and gentle. This is the least glamorous and most important block — Chapter 3 lives here.

steps.label: Build (weeks 7-12)
steps.content: Structured intensity arrives: threshold and VO2max work sharpen the engine the base built. Volume holds or edges down as intensity climbs. B-events slot in here as dress rehearsals.

steps.label: Peak (weeks 13-15)
steps.content: The hardest, most race-specific work: efforts that mimic the course's actual demands — long climbs at target pace, or repeated punchy efforts for a classics-style course.

steps.label: Taper (final 7-10 days)
steps.content: Volume drops 40-60%; short, sharp openers keep the legs awake. You cannot add fitness now — only reveal what you built. Chapter 7 covers the whole week.

steps.label: Race day
steps.content: Execution: pacing, fueling, and positioning. Chapters 5 and 6 earn their keep. The result was mostly decided in the previous 15 weeks — today you just collect it.

blocks.content: Count backwards before you register. Event date, minus taper, minus build, minus base — if the arithmetic lands before today, you're not picking a goal, you're scheduling a bad day. Pick a later event or a kinder course. Both count as smart, neither counts as quitting.
Be honest about the climbing. The single biggest predictor of how your day goes on a hilly course is your weight-adjusted threshold. If the route climbs, the plan climbs.

Here's the physics, without flinching: on a steep gradient, aerodynamics fade and gravity takes over, so speed becomes almost purely {{W/kg}} — your sustainable watts divided by everything you're hauling uphill. Two riders with identical 250 W thresholds climb very differently at 65 kg and 85 kg. That's not a moral judgment; it's arithmetic. It means a mountain fondo asks a different question than a flat one, and you should know your answer before you register, not at the base of the first col.

The good news: both sides of the fraction are trainable, and the watts side responds faster than most riders expect (Chapter 3). The other good news: courses publish their profiles. Nobody has to be ambushed by 5,000 metres of climbing they could have read about in January.

And check the time cuts. The big alpine events enforce them at intermediate points, not just the finish — the {{broom wagon}} works to a schedule. If the cut math looks tight for your current speed, that's your training target for the next four months, or your cue to pick the shorter course option most fondos offer. Riding the medio instead of the gran is how experienced riders handle an honest mismatch. It beats a DNF collected in a van.

blocks.question: You're choosing between two events: 138 km with 4,230 m of climbing, or 241 km with 2,260 m. Which is the harder climbing day?

options.text: The 241 km event — it's much longer and total fatigue is what matters
The 138 km event — at over 30 m of climbing per kilometre, it's a mountain race; the longer course is a rouleur's race
They're equivalent — climbing totals within 2,000 m of each other ride the same

blocks.explanation: Climbing density beats climbing total. 4,230 m in 138 km means the road is essentially never flat — your day is a chain of long cols ridden at threshold-adjacent effort, and W/kg decides everything. 2,260 m spread across 241 km is a long endurance day with punchy interruptions, where the draft, positioning, and durability matter more than raw climbing power. These are the real numbers for the Maratona dles Dolomites and the Tour of Flanders Sportive.

blocks.content: Every race this guide links to comes from our database of scored road events. Each one is rated across 14 dimensions — distance, climbing, logistics, prestige, organization, scenic experience, field depth, value, and more — and the scores are earned, not sponsored. Famous races land in Tier 2 all the time. That's the point: a rating you can't disagree with is a rating that isn't saying anything.

blocks.context: Of 395 rated road races earn Tier 1 status. The bar is deliberately high.

blocks.caption: Two Tier 1 races, two different sports. The Maratona is 138 km of Dolomite passes; Flanders is 241 km of cobbles and short, violent bergs. The tier tells you they're both worth your season — the dimensions tell you which one fits your engine.

blocks.content: Use the tiers to shortlist and the dimensions to decide. A Tier 1 badge means the whole package — course, organization, experience — justifies building a season around it. The dimension scores tell you whether *your* season should be the one.

The single-A-event rule survives because it works. One goal event gives the entire season a spine: every block, every long ride, every recovery week exists in service of one date. Riders who chase three "A" events a season usually arrive at all three in the same state — half-built, half-rested, and wholly annoyed about it.

items.label: Pick the A-event
items.detail: One date, one course, chosen against your engine and your calendar using everything above.

items.label: Anchor the plan to it
items.detail: Count backwards from race day to lay out base, build, peak, and taper. The date dictates the plan — never the reverse.

items.label: Slot B-events as rehearsals
items.detail: One or two, placed in the build phase. Ride them hard, test your fueling and pacing, and treat the result as data, not identity.

items.label: Protect the goal
items.detail: When life compresses training, the B-event is what gets sacrificed. The A-event only moves for weddings and surgeons.

blocks.content: B-events answer questions the plan can't: Does your fueling survive race intensity? Can you hold position in a real pack? Does your pacing discipline hold when adrenaline argues otherwise? A B-event that goes badly is a gift — the same lesson at your A-event would have cost you the season.
A starting point, not a verdict — every result below is a rated race from the database, so follow the link and read the dimensions before you commit a season to it.
